name: Middle temporal gyrus, temporo-occipital part
summary: The temporo-occipital part of the middle temporal gyrus is the posterior end of the gyrus where the temporal lobe merges with the lateral occipital lobe, behind the level of the atrium. It contains the human motion complex (area MT/V5 and its satellites) on its lateral surface and cortex that links visual form with meaning and with reading. It sits at the border of the middle and posterior cerebral artery territories, a watershed, and its damage causes akinetopsia, impaired perception of biological motion and, on the left, difficulties in reading and in retrieving words from pictures; seizures here produce elementary moving visual hallucinations.

anatomy.location: Posterior end of the middle temporal gyrus at the temporo-occipital junction, bounded above by the angular gyrus and the superior temporal sulcus, below by the inferior temporal gyrus, and behind by the lateral occipital cortex.

efferents.to: Frontal eye field and pontine pursuit centers

function: Area MT/V5 here receives direct magnocellular input from the primary visual cortex and from the pulvinar and computes the direction and speed of moving objects and the global motion of the visual scene; neighboring cortex in the superior temporal sulcus reads biological motion, gaze and gestures, and the ventral part links visual objects and written words to the semantic system of the middle temporal gyrus. Lesions produce loss of motion perception with preserved acuity and form vision, difficulty following moving conversation partners, and in the dominant hemisphere a slowing of reading. The region also guides smooth pursuit eye movements toward the ipsilateral side.

bestView.label: temporo-occipital junction of the middle temporal gyrus
lateral temporo-occipital cortex behind the atrium

imaging.normalAppearance: The lateral cortex just in front of the occipital lobe on axial images through the atria; the ascending limb of the inferior temporal sulcus is the landmark for the motion area.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion at the temporo-occipital junction along the border zone, with impaired motion perception or reading and a contralateral quadrantic field defect.
Bilateral temporo-parieto-occipital atrophy with preserved medial temporal lobes in a patient with visuospatial and reading difficulties.
Elementary moving visual hallucinations or a sense that the scene moves, with a posterior temporal EEG focus.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the MT/V5 motion complex on both sides

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral hemifield motion and pursuit deficits
lesionEffects.mechanism: Unilateral loss of MT/V5 and its projection to the pursuit system
Disconnection of visual word and object forms from the semantic system

examination: Ask the patient to follow a slowly moving target and to report moving objects in each hemifield
Timed reading of a paragraph and naming of pictures
Visual fields, including quadrants, by confrontation
pearls: Akinetopsia is rare but unmistakable: pouring tea looks like a frozen arc
The temporo-occipital junction is a watershed; hypotension picks it out in both hemispheres
Smooth pursuit toward one side depends on the temporo-occipital cortex of that side

pitfalls: Motion-selective deficits are not tested by standard perimetry; ask about moving objects and cars
